'''Cyberwarfare''' is the use of [[cyberattack]]s against an enemy [[state (polity)|state]], causing comparable harm to traditional [[warfare]].<ref>{{cite book |title=Cybersecurity and cyberwar: what everyone needs to know |last1=Singer|first1=P. W. |last2=Friedman|first2=Allan |date=March 2014 |isbn=978-0-19-991809-6 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |oclc=802324804}}</ref> Some intended outcomes could be [[cyber espionage|espionage]], [[sabotage]], [[propaganda]], [[Internet manipulation|manipulation]], or [[economic warfare]].

Many countries, including the [[United States]], [[United Kingdom]], [[Russia]], [[China]], [[Israel]], [[Iran]], [[India]], and [[North Korea]], have active cyber capabilities for offensive and defensive operations. As states explore the use of cyber operations and combine capabilities, the likelihood of physical confrontation and violence playing out as a result of, or part of, a cyber operation is increased. However, meeting the scale and protracted nature of war is unlikely, thus ambiguity remains.<ref name=":0">{{cite book |title=Cyber warfare: a multidisciplinary analysis |editor-last=Green|editor-first=James A. |isbn=978-0-415-78707-9 |location=London |publisher=[[Routledge]] |oclc=980939904 |date= 2016-11-07}}</ref>

There has been significant debate among experts regarding the definition of cyberwarfare, and even if such a thing exists.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://nato.int/docu/review/2013/Cyber/Cyberwar-does-it-exist/EN/index.htm |title=Cyberwar – does it exist? |date=2019-06-13 |publisher=[[NATO]] |access-date=2019-05-10}}</ref> One view is that the term is a misnomer, since no cyberattack to date could be described as a war.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Smith|first=Troy E. |date=2013 |title=Cyber Warfare: A Misrepresentation of the True Cyber Threat |journal=American Intelligence Journal |volume=31 |issue=1 |pages=82–85 |jstor=26202046 |issn=0883-072X}}</ref> An alternative view is that it is a suitable label for cyberattacks that cause physical damage to people and objects in the real world.<ref>{{cite book |title=Ethics and Cyber Warfare: The Quest for Responsible Security in the Age of Digital Warfare |last=Lucas|first=George |isbn=978-0-19-027652-2 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |page=6 |year=2017}}</ref>

The first instance of [[kinetic military action]] used in response to a cyberattack resulting in the loss of human life was observed on 5 May 2019, when the [[Israel Defense Forces]] targeted and destroyed a building associated with an ongoing cyberattack.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://wired.com/story/israel-hamas-cyberattack-air-strike-cyberwar |title=What Israel's Strike on Hamas Hackers Means for Cyberwar |last=Newman|first=Lily Hay |date=2019-05-06 |magazine=[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]] |access-date=2019-05-10 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://theverge.com/2019/5/5/18530412/israel-defense-force-hamas-cyber-attack-air-strike |title=Israel launched an airstrike in response to a Hamas cyberattack |last=Liptak|first=Andrew |date=2019-05-05 |website=[[The Verge]] |access-date=2019-05-10}}</ref>

== Definition ==
There is ongoing debate over how cyberwarfare should be defined and no absolute definition is widely agreed upon.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="Robinson">{{cite journal |last1=Robinson |first1=Michael |last2=Jones |first2=Kevin |last3=Helge |first3=Janicke |date=2015 |title=Cyber Warfare Issues and Challenges |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/276248097 |journal=Computers and Security |volume=49 |pages=70–94 |doi=10.1016/j.cose.2014.11.007 |access-date=2020-01-07 }}</ref> While the majority of [[Scholar|scholars]], [[militaries]], and [[Government|governments]] use definitions that refer to state and state-sponsored actors,<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name="Clarke" /> other definitions may include non-state actors, such as [[terrorist groups]], companies, political or ideological extremist groups, [[hacktivist]]s, and transnational criminal organizations depending on the context of the work.<ref>{{cite news |url= http://www.paconsulting.com/introducing-pas-media-site/highlighting-pas-expertise-in-the-media/articles-quoting-pa-experts/financial-times-security-a-huge-challenge-from-china-russia-and-organised-crime-1-november-2011/ |title= Security: A huge challenge from China, Russia and organised crime |date= 1 November 2011 |newspaper= Financial Times |last1= Blitz |first1= James |access-date= 6 June 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150606203810/http://www.paconsulting.com/introducing-pas-media-site/highlighting-pas-expertise-in-the-media/articles-quoting-pa-experts/financial-times-security-a-huge-challenge-from-china-russia-and-organised-crime-1-november-2011/ |archive-date= 6 June 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |date=1999 |title= Can information warfare ever be just?|url=http://philpapers.org/rec/ARQCIW|journal=Ethics and Information Technology |volume=1 |issue=3 |pages= 203–212 |doi= 10.1023/A:1010066528521 |last1= Arquilla |first1=John|s2cid= 29263858|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Examples of definitions proposed by experts in the field are as follows.

{{blockquote|'Cyberwarfare' is used in a broad context to denote interstate use of technological force within computer networks in which information is stored, shared, or communicated online.<ref name=":0" />}}Raymond Charles Parks and David P. Duggan focused on analyzing cyberwarfare in terms of computer networks and pointed out that "Cyberwarfare is a combination of computer network attack and defense and special technical operations."<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Parks|first1=Raymond C.|last2=Duggan|first2=David P.|date=September 2011|title=Principles of Cyberwarfare|journal=IEEE Security & Privacy|volume=9|issue=5|pages=30–35|doi=10.1109/MSP.2011.138|bibcode=2011ISPri...9e..30P |s2cid=17374534|issn=1558-4046}}</ref> According to this perspective, the notion of cyber warfare brings a new paradigm into military doctrine. [[Paulo Shakarian]] and colleagues put forward the following definition of "cyber war" in 2013, drawing on [[Carl von Clausewitz|Clausewitz]]'s definition of war: "War is the continuation of politics by other means":<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|title=Introduction to cyber-warfare: a multidisciplinary approach|last1=Shakarian|first1=Paulo|publisher=Morgan Kaufmann Publishers – Elsevier|last2=Shakarian |first2=Jana |last3=Ruef |first3=Andrew|year=2013|isbn=978-0-12-407926-7|location=Amsterdam |page=2 |oclc=846492852}}</ref>{{blockquote|Cyber war is an extension of policy by actions taken in cyber space by state or nonstate actors that constitute a serious threat to a nation's security or are conducted in response to a perceived threat against a nation's security.}}

Taddeo offered the following definition in 2012:
{{blockquote|The warfare grounded on certain uses of ICTs within an offensive or defensive military strategy endorsed by a state and aiming at the immediate disruption or control of the enemy's resources, and which is waged within the informational environment, with agents and targets ranging both on the physical and non-physical domains and whose level of violence may vary upon circumstances.<ref>{{cite conference |url=https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/6243976 |title=An analysis for a just cyber warfare |last1=Taddeo |first1=Mariarosaria |date=2012-07-19 |publisher=IEEE |location=Estonia |conference=International Conference on Cyber Conflict (ICCC)}}</ref>}}

Robinson et al. proposed in 2015 that the intent of the attacker dictates whether an attack is warfare or not, defining cyber warfare as "the use of cyber attacks with a warfare-like intent."<ref name="Robinson" />

In 2010, the former US National Coordinator for Security, Infrastructure Protection and Counter-terrorism, [[Richard A. Clarke]], defined cyberwarfare as "actions by a nation-state to penetrate another nation's computers or networks for the purposes of causing damage or disruption".<ref name="Clarke">Clarke, Richard A. ''Cyber War'', HarperCollins (2010) {{ISBN|978-0-06-196223-3}}</ref> The target's own cyber-physical infrastructure may be used by the adversary in case of a cyber conflict, thus weaponizing it.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.jinfowar.com/journal/volume-17-issue-4/implications-privacy-security-research-upcoming-battlefield-things|title=Implications of Privacy & Security Research for the Upcoming Battlefield of Things |journal=Journal of Information Warfare |volume=17 |issue=4 |year=2018 |access-date=2019-12-06}}</ref>

=== Controversy of term ===
There is debate on whether the term "cyber warfare" is accurate. In 2012, [[Eugene Kaspersky]], founder of [[Kaspersky Lab]], concluded that "[[cyberterrorism]]" is a more accurate term than "cyberwar." He states that "with today's attacks, you are clueless about who did it or when they will strike again. It's not cyber-war, but cyberterrorism."<ref name="Kaspersky1">[http://www.timesofisrael.com/experts-we-lost-the-cyber-war-now-were-in-the-era-of-cyber-terror/ "Latest viruses could mean 'end of the world as we know it,' says the man who discovered Flame"], ''The Times of Israel'', 6 June 2012</ref> [[Howard Schmidt]], former Cyber Security Coordinator in the [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Obama administration]], said that "there is no cyberwar... I think that is a terrible metaphor and I think that is a terrible concept. There are no winners in that environment."<ref name="Wired" />

Some experts take issue with the possible consequences linked to the warfare goal. In 2011, Ron Deibert, of Canada's [[Citizen Lab]], warned of a "[[militarization of cyberspace]]", as militaristic responses may not be appropriate.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Deibert|first=Ron|year=2011|title=Tracking the emerging arms race in cyberspace|url=http://bos.sagepub.com/content/67/1/1|journal=[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]]|volume=67|issue=1|pages=1–8|doi=10.1177/0096340210393703|s2cid=218770788|url-access=subscription}}</ref> However, to date, even serious cyber-attacks that have disrupted large parts of a nation's electrical grid (230,000 customers, [[December 2015 Ukraine power grid cyberattack|Ukraine, 2015]]) or affected access to medical care, thus endangering life (UK [[National Health Service]], [[WannaCry ransomware attack|WannaCry, 2017]]) have not led to military action.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-06-28 |title=What limits does the law of war impose on cyber attacks? |publisher=[[International Committee of the Red Cross]] |url=https://www.icrc.org/en/doc/resources/documents/faq/130628-cyber-warfare-q-and-a-eng.htm |access-date=2022-11-08 }}</ref>

In 2017, [[University of Oxford|Oxford]] academic Lucas Kello proposed a new term, "Unpeace", to denote highly damaging cyber actions whose non-violent effects do not rise to the level of traditional war. Such actions are neither warlike nor peace-like. Although they are non-violent, and thus not acts of war, their damaging effects on the economy and society may be greater than those of some armed attacks.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300220230/virtual-weapon-and-international-order|title=The Virtual Weapon and International Order|last=Kello|first=Lucas|date=2017|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=978-0-300-22023-0|location=New Haven, Connecticut|pages=77–79}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.-->|date=26 August 2017|title=The Politics of Cyberspace: Grasping the Danger|url=https://www.economist.com/news/books-and-arts/21727048-academia-still-grappling-problems-beset-computers-and-networks|magazine=[[The Economist]]|location=London}}</ref> This term is closely related to the concept of the "[[Grey-zone (international relations)|grey zone]]", which came to prominence in 2017, describing hostile actions that fall below the traditional threshold of war.<ref>{{Cite web|first1=George |last1=Popp |first2=Sarah |last2=Canna |title=The Characterization and Conditions of the Gray Zone|url=http://nsiteam.com/social/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/Final_NSI-ViTTa-Analysis_The-Characterization-and-Conditions-of-the-Gray-Zone.pdf |publisher=NSI, Inc.|date=Winter 2016|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210905011953/http://nsiteam.com/social/wp-content/uploads/2017/01/Final_NSI-ViTTa-Analysis_The-Characterization-and-Conditions-of-the-Gray-Zone.pdf |archive-date=5 September 2021 }}</ref> But as Kello explained, technological unpeace differs from the grey zone as the term is commonly used in that unpeace by definition is never overtly violent or fatal, whereas some grey-zone actions are violent, even if they are not acts of war.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=EaCCEAAAQBAJ&q=gray+zone|title=Striking Back: The End of Peace in Cyberspace and How to Restore It|last=Kello|first=Lucas|date=2022|publisher=Yale University Press|isbn=978-0-300-24668-1|location=New Haven, Connecticut|page=218}}</ref>

=== Cyberwarfare vs. cyber war ===
The term "cyberwarfare" is distinct from the term "cyber war". Cyberwarfare includes techniques, tactics and procedures that may be involved in a cyber war, but the term does not imply scale, protraction or violence, which are typically associated with the term "war", which inherently refers to a large-scale action, typically over a protracted period of time, and may include objectives seeking to utilize violence or the aim to kill.<ref name=":0" /> A cyber war could accurately describe a protracted period of back-and-forth cyber attacks (including in combination with traditional military action) between warring states. To date, no such action is known to have occurred. Instead, armed forces have responded with [[Tit for tat|tit-for-tat]] military cyber actions. For example, in June 2019, the United States launched a cyber attack against Iranian weapons systems in retaliation to the shooting down of a US drone in the [[Strait of Hormuz]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-48735097|title=US 'launched cyber-attack on Iran weapons systems'|date=2019-06-23|access-date=2019-08-09|website=[[BBC News]]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/22/us/politics/us-iran-cyber-attacks.html|title=U.S. Carried Out Cyberattacks on Iran|last1=Barnes|first1=Julian E.|date=2019-06-22|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2019-08-09|last2=Gibbons-Neff|first2=Thomas|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

=== Cyberwarfare and cyber sanctions ===
In addition to retaliatory digital attacks, countries can respond to cyber attacks with [[cyber sanctions]]. Sometimes, it is not easy to detect the attacker, but suspicions may focus on a particular country or group of countries. In these cases, unilateral and multilateral economic sanctions can be used instead of cyberwarfare. For example, the United States has frequently imposed economic sanctions related to cyber attacks. Two [[Executive Order]]s issued during the [[Presidency of Barack Obama|Obama administration]], EO 13694 of 2015<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-04-01|title=Executive Order – "Blocking the Property of Certain Persons Engaging in Significant Malicious Cyber-Enabled Activities"|url=https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/2015/04/01/executive-order-blocking-property-certain-persons-engaging-significant-m|access-date=2021-06-19|website=The White House}}</ref> and EO 13757 of 2016,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Sanctions Programs and Country Information |website=U.S. Department of the Treasury|url=https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/sanctions-programs-and-country-information|access-date=2021-06-19}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Cyber Sanctions|url=https://www.state.gov/cyber-sanctions/|access-date=2021-06-19|website=United States Department of State}}</ref> specifically focused on the implementation of the cyber sanctions. Subsequent US presidents have issued similar Executive Orders. The [[United States Congress|US Congress]] has also imposed cyber sanctions in response to cyberwarfare. For example, the Iran Cyber Sanctions Act of 2016 imposes sanctions on specific individuals responsible for cyber attacks.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ratcliffe|first=John|date=2016-05-18|title=Text – H.R.5222 – 114th Congress (2015–2016): Iran Cyber Sanctions Act of 2016|url=https://www.congress.gov/bill/114th-congress/house-bill/5222/text|access-date=2021-06-19|website=United States Congress}}</ref>

== Types of warfare ==
Cyber warfare can present a multitude of threats towards a nation. At the most basic level, cyber attacks can be used to support traditional warfare. For example, tampering with the operation of air defenses via cyber means in order to facilitate an air attack.<ref>{{cite magazine |last=Weinberger |first=Sharon |title=How Israel Spoofed Syria's Air Defense System |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2007/10/how-israel-spoo/ |date=4 October 2007}}</ref> Aside from these "hard" threats, cyber warfare can also contribute towards "soft" threats such as espionage and propaganda.
[[Eugene Kaspersky]], founder of [[Kaspersky Lab]], equates large-scale [[cyber weapon]]s, such as [[Flame (malware)|Flame]] and [[NetTraveler]] which his company discovered, to [[biological weapons]], claiming that in an interconnected world, they have the potential to be equally destructive.<ref name="Kaspersky1" /><ref name="Kaspersky2">[http://www.timesofisrael.com/new-cyber-bug-targeting-middle-east-but-israel-untouched-so-far/ "Cyber espionage bug attacking Middle East, but Israel untouched — so far"], ''The Times of Israel'', 4 June 2013</ref>

=== Sabotage ===
Computers and [[satellites]] that coordinate other activities are vulnerable components of a system and could lead to the disruption of equipment. Compromise of military systems, such as [[C4ISTAR]] components that are responsible for orders and communications could lead to their interception or malicious replacement. Power, water, fuel, communications, and transportation infrastructure all may be vulnerable to disruption. According to Clarke, the civilian realm is also at risk, noting that the security breaches have already gone beyond stolen credit card numbers, and that potential targets can also include the electric power grid, trains, or the stock market.<ref name=Clark2>[http://www.hometownannapolis.com/news/top/2010/09/24-11/Clarke-More-defense-needed-in-cyberspace.html "Clarke: More defense needed in cyberspace"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324191031/http://www.hometownannapolis.com/news/top/2010/09/24-11/Clarke-More-defense-needed-in-cyberspace.html |date=24 March 2012 }} HometownAnnapolis.com, 24 September 2010</ref>

In mid-July 2010, security experts discovered a malicious software program called [[Stuxnet]] that had infiltrated factory computers and had spread to plants around the world. It is considered "the first attack on critical industrial infrastructure that sits at the foundation of modern economies," notes ''The New York Times''.<ref>[http://bits.blogs.nytimes.com/2010/09/24/malware-hits-computerized-industrial-equipment/ "Malware Hits Computerized Industrial Equipment"]. ''The New York Times'', 24 September 2010</ref>

[[Stuxnet]], while extremely effective in delaying [[Iran's nuclear program]] for the development of nuclear weaponry, came at a high cost. For the first time, it became clear that not only could cyber weapons be defensive but they could be offensive. The large decentralization and scale of cyberspace makes it extremely difficult to direct from a policy perspective. Non-state actors can play as large a part in the cyberwar space as state actors, which leads to dangerous, sometimes disastrous, consequences. Small groups of highly skilled malware developers are able to as effectively impact global politics and cyber warfare as large governmental agencies. A major aspect of this ability lies in the willingness of these groups to share their exploits and developments on the web as a form of arms proliferation. This allows lesser hackers to become more proficient in creating the large scale attacks that once only a small handful were skillful enough to manage. In addition, thriving black markets for these kinds of cyber weapons are buying and selling these cyber capabilities to the highest bidder without regard for consequences.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Singer |first1=P.W. |last2=Friedman |first2=Allan |date=2014 |title=Cybersecurity and Cyberwar: What Everyone Needs to Know |location=Oxford |publisher=Oxford University Press |page=156 |isbn=978-0-19-991809-6}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gross|first1=Michael L.|last2=Canetti|first2=Daphna|last3=Vashdi|first3=Dana R.|date=2016|title=The psychological effects of cyber terrorism|journal=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|volume=72|issue=5|pages=284–291|doi=10.1080/00963402.2016.1216502|issn=0096-3402|pmc=5370589|pmid=28366962|bibcode=2016BuAtS..72e.284G}}</ref>

==== Denial-of-service attack ====
{{Main|Denial-of-service attack}}
In computing, a denial-of-service attack ([[Denial-of-service attack|DoS]] attack) or distributed denial-of-service attack (DDoS attack) is an attempt to make a machine or network resource unavailable to its intended users. Perpetrators of DoS attacks typically target sites or services hosted on high-profile web servers such as banks, credit card payment gateways, and even root nameservers. DoS attacks often leverage internet-connected devices with vulnerable security measures to carry out these large-scale attacks.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Understanding Denial-of-Service Attacks {{!}} CISA|url=https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/tips/ST04-015|access-date=2020-10-10|website=us-cert.cisa.gov|archive-date=18 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210318061711/https://us-cert.cisa.gov/ncas/tips/ST04-015}}</ref> DoS attacks may not be limited to computer-based methods, as strategic physical attacks against infrastructure can be just as devastating. For example, cutting undersea communication cables may severely cripple some regions and countries with regards to their information warfare ability.<ref>{{Cite news |author=Sherryn Groch |author2=Felicity Lewis |date=2022-11-04 |title=The internet is run under the sea. What if the cables are cut? |url=https://www.smh.com.au/technology/the-internet-is-run-under-the-sea-not-in-the-cloud-what-happens-if-the-cables-get-hacked-or-snipped-20221025-p5bsov.html |access-date=2022-11-08 |newspaper=The Sydney Morning Herald |language=en}}</ref>

=== Propaganda ===
Cyber propaganda is an effort to control information in whatever form it takes, and influence public opinion.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-europe-39062663|title=Russian military admits significant cyber-war effort|date=21 February 2017|work=bbc.com}}</ref> It is a form of [[psychological warfare]], except it uses [[social media]], [[fake news website]]s and other digital means.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ajir|first1=Media|last2=Vailliant|first2=Bethany|date=2018|title=Russian Information Warfare: Implications for Deterrence Theory|journal=Strategic Studies Quarterly|volume=12|issue=3|pages=70–89|jstor=26481910|issn=1936-1815}}</ref> In 2018, Sir Nicholas Carter, Chief of the General Staff of the [[British Army]] stated that this kind of attack from actors such as Russia "is a form of system warfare that seeks to de-legitimize the political and social system on which our military strength is based".<ref>{{cite web |title=Dynamic Security Threats and the British Army |url=https://rusi.org/event/dynamic-security-threats-and-british-army |date=22 January 2018 |publisher=RUSI |last=Carter |first=Nicholas |access-date=30 January 2018 |archive-date=29 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180329141808/https://rusi.org/event/dynamic-security-threats-and-british-army }}</ref>

Jowell and O'Donnell (2006) state that "propaganda is the deliberate, systematic attempt to shape perceptions, manipulate cognitions, and direct behavior to achieve a response that furthers the desired intent of the propagandist" (p. 7). The internet is the most important means of communication today. People can convey their messages quickly across to a huge audience, and this can open a window for evil. Terrorist organizations can exploit this and may use this medium to brainwash people. It has been suggested that restricted media coverage of terrorist attacks would in turn decrease the number of terrorist attacks that occur afterwards.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cowen|first=Tyler|date=2006|title=Terrorism as Theater: Analysis and Policy Implications|journal=Public Choice|volume=128|issue=1/2|pages=233–244|doi=10.1007/s11127-006-9051-y|jstor=30026642|s2cid=155001568|issn=0048-5829}}</ref>

== Motivations ==
There are a number of reasons nations undertake offensive cyber operations. {{interlanguage link|Sandro Gaycken|de}}, a cyber security expert and adviser to [[NATO]], advocates that states take cyber warfare seriously as they are viewed as an attractive activity by many nations, in times of war and peace. Offensive cyber operations offer a large variety of cheap and risk-free options to weaken other countries and strengthen their own positions. Considered from a long-term, geostrategic perspective, cyber offensive operations can cripple whole economies, change political views, agitate conflicts within or among states, reduce their military efficiency and equalize the capacities of high-tech nations to that of low-tech nations, and use access to their critical infrastructures to blackmail them.<ref>{{cite book |last=Gaycken|first=Sandro|year=2010|title=Cyberwar – Das Internet als Kriegsschauplatz|url=https://www.opensourcepress.de/index.php?26&backPID=178&tt_products=313}}</ref>

=== Hacktivism ===
Politically motivated [[hacktivism]] involves the subversive use of computers and [[computer network]]s to promote an agenda, and can potentially extend to attacks, theft and virtual sabotage that could be seen as cyberwarfare – or mistaken for it.<ref>Denning, D. E. (2008). [http://faculty.nps.edu/dedennin/publications/Ethics%20of%20Cyber%20Conflict.pdf The ethics of cyber conflict. The Handbook of Information and Computer Ethics]. 407–429.</ref>
Hacktivists use their knowledge and software tools to gain unauthorized access to computer systems they seek to manipulate or damage not for material gain or to cause widespread destruction, but to draw attention to their cause through well-publicized disruptions of select targets. Anonymous and other hacktivist groups are often portrayed in the media as cyber-terrorists, wreaking havoc by hacking websites, posting sensitive information about their victims, and threatening further attacks if their demands are not met. However, hacktivism is more than that. Actors are politically motivated to change the world, through the use of fundamentalism. Groups like Anonymous, however, have divided opinion with their anarchic methods.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kenney|first1=Michael|title=Cyber-Terrorism in a Post-Stuxnet World|journal=Orbis|date=2015|volume=59|issue=1|pages=111–128|doi=10.1016/j.orbis.2014.11.009}}</ref>

=== Income generation ===
Cyber attacks, including ransomware, can be used to generate income. States can use these techniques to generate significant sources of income, which can evade sanctions and perhaps while simultaneously harming adversaries (depending on targets). This tactic was observed in August 2019 when it was revealed North Korea had generated $2 billion to fund its weapons program, avoiding the blanket of sanctions levied by the [[United States]], [[United Nations]] and the [[European Union]].<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-northkorea-cyber-un-idUSKCN1UV1ZX|title=North Korea took $2 billion in cyberattacks to fund weapons...|date=2019-08-05|work=Reuters|access-date=2019-08-09|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-49259302|title=North Korea 'stole $2bn via cyber-attacks'|date=2019-08-07|access-date=2019-08-09|language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Preparedness ==
A number of countries conduct exercise to increase preparedness and explore the strategy, tactics and operations involved in conducting and defending against cyber attacks against hostile states, this is typically done in the form of [[Wargame (hacking)|war games]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cyber-war gaming: A cybersecurity tabletop exercise |url=https://www.techtarget.com/searchsecurity/feature/Cyber-war-gaming-A-cybersecurity-tabletop-exercise |access-date=2022-11-08 |website=SearchSecurity |language=en}}</ref>

The [[Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence|Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence (CCDCE)]], part of the [[NATO|North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO)]], have conducted a yearly war game called Locked Shields since 2010 designed to test readiness and improve skills, strategy tactics and operational decision making of participating national organizations.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://ccdcoe.org/exercises/locked-shields/|title=Locked Shields|website=ccdcoe.org|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ncia.nato.int/NewsRoom/Pages/20190408-Lock-Shields.aspx|title=Agency leads NATO team in tough cyber exercise|website=www.ncia.nato.int|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref> Locked Shields 2019 saw 1200 participants from 30 countries compete in a [[red team]] vs. [[Blue team (computer security)|blue team]] exercise. The war game involved a fictional country, Berylia, which was "experiencing a deteriorating security situation, where a number of hostile events coincide with coordinated cyber attacks against a major civilian internet service provider and maritime surveillance system. The attacks caused severe disruptions in the power generation and distribution, 4G communication systems, maritime surveillance, water purification plant and other critical infrastructure components". CCDCE describe the aim of the exercise was to "maintain the operation of various systems under intense pressure, the strategic part addresses the capability to understand the impact of decisions made at the strategic and policy level."<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ukdefencejournal.org.uk/nato-takes-part-in-international-cyber-security-exercise/|title=NATO takes part in international cyber security exercise|last=Allison|first=George|date=2019-04-11|website=UK Defence Journal|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref> Ultimately, [[France]] was the winner of [[Locked Shields]] 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://ccdcoe.org/news/2019/france-wins-cyber-defence-exercise-locked-shields-2019/|title=CCDCOE|website=ccdcoe.org|access-date=2019-08-07}}</ref>

The [[European Union]] conducts cyber war game scenarios with member states and foreign partner states to improve readiness, skills and observe how strategic and tactical decisions may affect the scenario.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2019/jun/27/eu-war-games-prepare-russia-china-cyber-attacks|title=EU to run war games to prepare for Russian and Chinese cyber-attacks|last=Boffey|first=Daniel|date=2019-06-27|work=The Guardian|access-date=2019-08-07|language=en-GB|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

As well as war games which serve a broader purpose to explore options and improve skills, cyber war games are targeted at preparing for specific threats. In 2018 the Sunday Times reported the UK government was conducting cyber war games which could "blackout Moscow".<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/uk-war-games-cyber-attack-on-moscow-dgxz8ppv0|title=UK war-games cyber attack on Moscow|first1=Caroline|last1=Wheeler|first2=Tim|last2=Shipman|first3=Mark|last3=Hookham|date=2018-10-07|work=The Sunday Times|access-date=2019-08-08|language=en|issn=0956-1382}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://qz.com/1416362/the-uk-war-games-cyberattacks-that-could-black-out-moscow/|title=The UK is practicing cyberattacks that could black out Moscow|last=Detrixhe|first=John|website=Quartz|date=7 October 2018 |language=en|access-date=2019-08-08}}</ref> These types of war games move beyond defensive preparedness, as previously described above and onto preparing offensive capabilities which can be used as deterrence, or for "war".<ref>{{Cite news |date=2017-09-19 |title=Public servants prepare for cyber attacks at inaugural war games |language=en-AU |work=ABC News |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2017-09-20/government-workers-practice-cyber-attacks-in-inaugural-war-games/8961836 |access-date=2022-11-08}}</ref>

==== India ====
The Department of Information Technology created the [[Indian Computer Emergency Response Team]] (CERT-In) in 2004 to thwart cyber attacks in India.<ref name="businesstoday.intoday.in">{{cite news |url=http://businesstoday.intoday.in/story/india-cyber-security-at-risk/1/191786.html |title= Beware of the bugs: Can cyber attacks on India's critical infrastructure be thwarted? |work= BusinessToday |access-date= 15 January 2013 }}</ref> That year, there were 23 reported cyber security breaches. In 2011, there were 13,301. That year, the government created a new subdivision, the [[National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre]] (NCIIPC) to thwart attacks against energy, transport, banking, telecom, defense, space and other sensitive areas.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 8, 2022 |title=National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre |url=https://nciipc.gov.in/ |access-date=November 8, 2022 |website=National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre}}</ref>

The executive director of the [[Nuclear Power Corporation of India]] (NPCIL) stated in February 2013 that his company alone was forced to block up to ten targeted attacks a day. CERT-In was left to protect less critical sectors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Poornima |first=B. |date=August 2022 |title=Cyber Threats and Nuclear Security in India |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/23477970221099748 |journal=Journal of Asian Security and International Affairs |language=en |volume=9 |issue=2 |pages=183–206 |doi=10.1177/23477970221099748 |s2cid=249831452 |issn=2347-7970|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A high-profile cyber attack on 12 July 2012 breached the email accounts of about 12,000 people, including those of officials from the [[Ministry of External Affairs (India)|Ministry of External Affairs]], [[Ministry of Home Affairs (India)|Ministry of Home Affairs]], [[Defence Research and Development Organisation|Defense Research and Development Organizations]] (DRDO), and the [[Indo-Tibetan Border Police]] (ITBP).<ref name="businesstoday.intoday.in" /> A government-private sector plan being overseen by [[National Security Advisor (India)|National Security Advisor]] (NSA) [[Shivshankar Menon]] began in October 2012, and intends to boost up India's cyber security capabilities in the light of a group of experts findings that India faces a 470,000 shortfall of such experts despite the country's reputation of being an IT and software powerhouse.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/5-lakh-cyber-warriors-to-bolster-Indias-e-defence/articleshow/16828463.cms|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130126024048/http://articles.timesofindia.indiatimes.com/2012-10-16/india/34498075_1_cyber-security-cyber-attacks-cyber-warfare|url-status=live|archive-date=26 January 2013|title=5 lakh cyber warriors to bolster India's e-defence|date=16 October 2012|location=India|work=[[The Times of India]]|access-date=18 October 2012}}</ref>

In February 2013, Information Technology Secretary [[J. Satyanarayana]] stated that the [[National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre|NCIIPC]]{{page needed|date=November 2013}} was finalizing policies related to national cyber security that would focus on domestic security solutions, reducing exposure through foreign technology.<ref name="businesstoday.intoday.in" /> Other steps include the isolation of various security agencies to ensure that a synchronised attack could not succeed on all fronts and the planned appointment of a National Cyber Security Coordinator. As of that month, there had been no significant economic or physical damage to India related to cyber attacks.

On 26 November 2010, a group calling itself the Indian Cyber Army hacked the websites belonging to the Pakistan Army and the others belong to different ministries, including the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Ministry of Education, Ministry of Finance, Pakistan Computer Bureau, Council of Islamic Ideology, etc. The attack was done as a revenge for the [[Mumbai terrorist attacks]].<ref>[http://tribune.com.pk/story/83967/36-government-websites-hacked-by-indian-cyber-army/ "36 government sites hacked by 'Indian Cyber Army'"]. ''The Express Tribune''. Retrieved 8 November 2011.</ref>

On 4 December 2010, a group calling itself the Pakistan Cyber Army hacked the website of India's top investigating agency, the [[Central Bureau of Investigation]] (CBI). The [[National Informatics Center]] (NIC) has begun an inquiry.<ref>[http://www.ndtv.com/article/india/hacked-by-pakistan-cyber-army-cbi-website-still-not-restored-70568?cp "Hacked by 'Pakistan cyber army', CBI website still not restored"]. Ndtv.com (4 December 2010). Retrieved 8 November 2011.</ref>

In July 2016, Cymmetria researchers discovered and revealed the cyber attack dubbed 'Patchwork', which compromised an estimated 2500 corporate and government agencies using code stolen from [[GitHub]] and the [[dark web]]. Examples of weapons used are an exploit for the Sandworm vulnerability ({{CVE|2014–4114}}), a compiled AutoIt script, and UAC bypass code dubbed UACME. Targets are believed to be mainly military and political assignments around Southeast Asia and the South China Sea and the attackers are believed to be of Indian origin and gathering intelligence from influential parties.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2016/07/08/copy_paste_slacker_hackers_pop_corp_locks_in_ode_to_stolen_code/|title=Copy paste slacker hackers pop corp locks in ode to stolen code|website=The Register|last1=Pauli|first1=Darren |date=8 July 2016 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://threatpost.com/apt-group-patchwork-cuts-and-pastes-a-potent-attack/119081/|title=APT Group 'Patchwork' Cuts-and-Pastes a Potent Attack|date=7 July 2016|publisher=Threatpost|access-date=2 January 2017}}</ref>

The [[Defence Cyber Agency]], which is the Indian military agency responsible for cyberwarfare, has been fully operational since August 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |last=SNS |date=2021-08-04 |title='GOI in final stage of formulating National Cyber Security strategy' |url=https://www.thestatesman.com/india/goi-national-cyber-security-strategy-1502990178.html |access-date=2026-03-28 |website=The Statesman |language=en}}</ref>

Some of the companies used in the attack were partially owned by several governments, further complicating [[cyber attribution]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j4pF9VUdphc |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211221/j4pF9VUdphc |archive-date=2021-12-21 |url-status=live|title=28c3: Security Log Visualization with a Correlation Engine|website=[[YouTube]]|date= 29 December 2011|access-date= 4 November 2017}}{{cbignore}}</ref>
In July 2011, the South Korean company [[SK Communications]] was hacked, resulting in the theft of the personal details (including names, phone numbers, home and email addresses and resident registration numbers) of up to 35 million people. A trojaned software update was used to gain access to the SK Communications network. Links exist between this hack and other malicious activity and it is believed to be part of a broader, concerted hacking effort.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.commandfive.com/papers/C5_APT_SKHack.pdf|title=SK Hack by an Advanced Persistent Threat|publisher=Command Five Pty Ltd|access-date=24 September 2011}}</ref>

With ongoing tensions on the Korean Peninsula, [[Ministry of National Defense (Republic of Korea)|South Korea's defense ministry]] stated that South Korea was going to improve cyber-defense strategies in hopes of preparing itself from possible cyber attacks. In March 2013, South Korea's major banks – Shinhan Bank, Woori Bank and NongHyup Bank – as well as many broadcasting stations – KBS, YTN and MBC – were hacked and more than 30,000 computers were affected; it is one of the biggest attacks South Korea has faced in years.<ref name="Global Post">{{cite web|url=http://www.globalpost.com/dispatch/news/thomson-reuters/130320/south-korea-police-investigating-server-outages-at-major-tv-net|title=South Korea raises alert after hackers attack broadcasters, banks|last=Lee|first=Se Young|work=Global Post|date=20 March 2013 |access-date=6 April 2013}}</ref> Although it remains uncertain as to who was involved in this incident, there has been immediate assertions that North Korea is connected, as it threatened to attack South Korea's government institutions, major national banks and traditional newspapers numerous times – in reaction to the sanctions it received from nuclear testing and to the continuation of [[Foal Eagle]], South Korea's annual joint military exercise with the United States. North Korea's cyber warfare capabilities raise the alarm for South Korea, as North Korea is increasing its manpower through military academies specializing in hacking. Current figures state that South Korea only has 400 units of specialized personnel, while North Korea has more than 3,000 highly trained hackers; this portrays a huge gap in cyber warfare capabilities and sends a message to South Korea that it has to step up and strengthen its Cyber Warfare Command forces. Therefore, in order to be prepared from future attacks, South Korea and the United States will discuss further about deterrence plans at the Security Consultative Meeting (SCM). At SCM, they plan on developing strategies that focuses on accelerating the deployment of ballistic missiles as well as fostering its defense shield program, known as the Korean Air and Missile Defense.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://english.yonhapnews.co.kr/national/2013/04/01/20/0301000000AEN20130401004000315F.HTML|title=S. Korean military to prepare with U.S. for cyber warfare scenarios|last=Kim|first=Eun-jung|agency=Yonhap News Agency|access-date=6 April 2013|date=April 2013}}</ref>

==== Ukraine ====
According to [[CrowdStrike]] from 2014 to 2016, the Russian APT [[Fancy Bear]] used Android malware to target the Ukrainian Army's [[Rocket Forces and Artillery (Ukraine)|Rocket Forces and Artillery]]. They distributed an infected version of an [[Android (operating system)|Android]] [[Mobile app|app]] whose original purpose was to control targeting data for the [[122 mm howitzer 2A18 (D-30)|D-30 Howitzer]] artillery. The app, used by Ukrainian officers, was loaded with the [[X Agent (spyware)|X-Agent]] spyware and posted online on military forums. The attack was claimed by Crowd-Strike to be successful, with more than 80% of Ukrainian D-30 Howitzers destroyed, the highest percentage loss of any artillery pieces in the army (a percentage that had never been previously reported and would mean the loss of nearly the entire arsenal of the biggest artillery piece of the [[Ukrainian Armed Forces]]<ref>[https://www.yahoo.com/news/ukraines-military-denies-russian-hack-attack-143419289.html Ukraine's military denies Russian hack attack] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170107101109/https://www.yahoo.com/news/ukraines-military-denies-russian-hack-attack-143419289.html |date=7 January 2017 }} , [[Yahoo! News]] (6 January 2017)</ref>).<ref name="CrowdStrike">{{cite web|url=https://www.crowdstrike.com/blog/danger-close-fancy-bear-tracking-ukrainian-field-artillery-units/|title=Danger Close: Fancy Bear Tracking of Ukrainian Field Artillery Units|date=22 December 2016|publisher=CrowdStrike}}</ref> According to the [[Ukrainian army]] this number is incorrect and that losses in artillery weapons "were way below those reported" and that these losses "have nothing to do with the stated cause".<ref>[http://en.interfax.com.ua/news/general/395186.html Defense ministry denies reports of alleged artillery losses because of Russian hackers' break into software], [[Interfax-Ukraine]] (6 January 2017)</ref>

In 2014, the Russians were suspected to use a cyber weapon called "[[Snake (malware)|Snake]]", or "Ouroboros," to conduct a cyber attack on Ukraine during a period of political turmoil. The Snake tool kit began spreading into Ukrainian computer systems in 2010. It performed Computer Network Exploitation (CNE), as well as highly sophisticated Computer Network Attacks (CNA).<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Evolution of Cyber War|last=Mazanec|first=Brain M.|publisher=University of Nebraska Press|year=2015|isbn=978-1-61234-763-9|location=USA|pages=221–222}}</ref>

On 23 December 2015 the [[BlackEnergy|Black-Energy]] malware was used in [[December 2015 Ukraine power grid cyber attack|a cyberattack on Ukraine's power-grid]] that left more than 200,000 people temporarily without power. A mining company and a large railway operator were also victims of the attack.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theregister.co.uk/2016/03/04/ukraine_blackenergy_confirmation/|title=BlackEnergy malware activity spiked in runup to Ukraine power grid takedown|website=The Register|date=4 March 2016 |access-date=26 December 2016}}</ref>

Ukraine saw a massive surge in cyber attacks during the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]]. ==== Saudi Arabia ====
On 15 August 2012 at 11:08 am local time, the [[Shamoon]] virus began destroying over 35,000 computer systems, rendering them inoperable. The virus used to target the [[Saudi Arabia|Saudi]] government by causing destruction to the state owned national oil company [[Saudi Aramco]]. The attackers posted a pastie on PasteBin.com hours prior to the wiper logic bomb occurring, citing oppression and the [[Al-Saud regime]] as a reason behind the attack.<ref>{{cite web |id= Cutting Sword of Justice |title= Pastie: 'Untitled' |url= https://pastebin.com/HqAgaQRj |access-date=3 November 2017 |date= 15 August 2012}}</ref>  The attack was well staged according to [[Chris Kubecka]], a former security advisor to Saudi Aramco after the attack and group leader of security for Aramco Overseas.<ref>{{cite news|title=Jose Pagliery:The inside story of the biggest hack in history |url= https://money.cnn.com/2015/08/05/technology/aramco-hack/index.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150808020211/http://money.cnn.com/2015/08/05/technology/aramco-hack/index.html |url-status= dead |archive-date= 8 August 2015 |work= [[CNN Money]] |date=5 August 2015 |access-date= 15 May 2019}}</ref> It was an unnamed Saudi Aramco employee on the Information Technology team which opened a malicious phishing email, allowing initial entry into the computer network around mid-2012.<ref name=Kubecka>{{cite news |title= How to Implement IT Security after a Cyber Meltdown |url= https://www.blackhat.com/docs/us-15/materials/us-15-Kubecka-How-To-Implement-IT-Security-After-A-Cyber-Meltdown.pdf |date= 29 December 2015 |first= Christina|last= Kubecka|access-date= 3 November 2017}} ({{youTube|WyMobr_TDSI}}-[https://archive.org/details/youtube-WyMobr_TDSI archive])</ref>
Kubecka also detailed in her Black Hat USA talk Saudi Aramco placed the majority of their security budget on the ICS control network, leaving the business network at risk for a major incident.<ref name=Kubecka/> The virus has been noted to have behavior differing from other malware attacks, due to the destructive nature and the cost of the attack and recovery. US Defense Secretary [[Leon Panetta]] called the attack a "Cyber Pearl Harbor".<ref>{{cite news |title= Elisabeth Bumiller and Thom Shanker: Panetta Warns of Dire Threat of Cyberattack on U.S. |newspaper= The New York Times |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2012/10/12/world/panetta-warns-of-dire-threat-of-cyberattack.html |date= 11 October 2012 |access-date=3 November 2017 |last1= Bumiller |first1= Elisabeth |last2= Shanker |first2= Thom }}</ref> Shamoon can spread from an infected machine to [[Computer data storage#Network connectivity|other computers on the network]]. Once a system is infected, the virus continues to compile a list of files from specific locations on the system, upload them to the attacker, and erase them. Finally the virus overwrites the [[master boot record]] of the infected computer, making it unusable.<ref name="symantec"/><ref>{{cite news|title=Jose Pagliery: The inside story of the biggest hack in history|url=https://money.cnn.com/2015/08/05/technology/aramco-hack/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150808020211/http://money.cnn.com/2015/08/05/technology/aramco-hack/index.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=8 August 2015|date=5 August 2015|access-date=19 August 2012}}</ref> The virus has been used for [[cyber warfare]] against the national oil companies Saudi Aramco and Qatar's [[RasGas]].<ref>{{cite news |first= Michael |last= Harper |title= RedOrbit: Energy Company RasGas Is Infected with Shamoon Virus |date= 31 August 2012}}</ref><ref name="dj">{{cite news |url= http://www.digitaljournal.com/article/331033 |title=Shamoon virus attacks Saudi oil company |work= Digital Journal |date= 18 August 2012 |access-date= 19 August 2012}}</ref><ref name="symantec">{{cite web |url= https://community.broadcom.com/symantecenterprise/communities/community-home/librarydocuments/viewdocument?DocumentKey=281521ea-2d18-4bf9-9e88-8b1dc41cfdb6&CommunityKey=1ecf5f55-9545-44d6-b0f4-4e4a7f5f5e68&tab=librarydocuments |title= The Shamoon Attacks |publisher= Symantec |date= 16 August 2012 |access-date= 19 August 2012}}</ref><ref name="bbc">{{cite news |url= https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/technology-19293797 |title= Shamoon virus targets energy sector infrastructure |work= [[BBC News]] |date= 17 August 2012 |access-date= 19 August 2012}}</ref>

Saudi Aramco announced the attack on their Facebook page and went offline again until a company statement was issued on 25 August 2012. The statement falsely reported normal business was resumed on 25 August 2012. However a Middle Eastern journalist leaked photographs taken on 1 September 2012 showing kilometers of petrol trucks unable to be loaded due to backed business systems still inoperable.
On 29 August 2012 the same attackers behind Shamoon posted another pastie on PasteBin.com, taunting Saudi Aramco with proof they still retained access to the company network. The post contained the username and password on security and network equipment and the new password for the CEO Khalid Al- Falih<ref>{{cite web |url=https://pastebin.com/AtN7dLeW |title= Saudi Aramco hug, another one |date= 29 August 2012 |access-date= 3 November 2017}}</ref> The attackers also referenced a portion of the Shamoon malware as further proof in the pastie.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-12-19 |title=Shamoon Attackers Employ New Tool Kit to Wipe Infected Systems |url=https://www.mcafee.com/blogs/other-blogs/mcafee-labs/shamoon-attackers-employ-new-tool-kit-to-wipe-infected-systems/ |access-date=2022-11-08 |website=McAfee Blog |language=en-US}}</ref>

According to Kubecka, in order to restore operations. Saudi Aramco used its large private fleet of aircraft and available funds to purchase much of the world's hard drives, driving the price up. New hard drives were required as quickly as possible so oil prices were not affected by speculation. By 1 September 2012 gasoline resources were dwindling for the public of Saudi Arabia 17 days after the 15 August attack. [[RasGas]] was also affected by a different variant, crippling them in a similar manner.<ref>{{cite web |title= Youtube – Chris Kubecka: How to Implement IT Security after a Cyber Meltdown |website = [[YouTube]]|url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WyMobr_TDSI |date= 3 August 2015 |access-date= 3 November 2017}}</ref>

== Cyberpeace ==
{{See also|Cyberweapon#Control and disarmament}}
The rise of cyber as a warfighting domain has led to efforts to determine how cyberspace can be used to foster peace.  For example, the German civil rights panel [[:de:Forum InformatikerInnen für Frieden und gesellschaftliche Verantwortung|FIfF]] runs a campaign for cyberpeace − for the control of cyberweapons and surveillance technology and against the militarization of cyberspace and the development and stockpiling of offensive exploits and malware.<ref name=fiff>{{cite book|last1=Hofkirchner|first1=Wolfgang|last2=Burgin|first2=Mark|title=The Future Information Society: Social and Technological Problems|publisher=World Scientific|isbn=978-981-310-898-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fPmtDgAAQBAJ&pg=PA459|access-date=22 May 2017|language=en|date=2017-01-24}}</ref> Measures for cyberpeace include policymakers developing new rules and norms for warfare, individuals and organizations building new tools and secure infrastructures, promoting [[open source software|open source]], the establishment of cyber security centers, auditing of critical infrastructure cybersecurity, obligations to disclose vulnerabilities, disarmament, defensive security strategies, decentralization, education and widely applying relevant tools and infrastructures, encryption and other cyberdefenses.<ref name=fiff/><ref>{{cite book|last1=Grady|first1=Mark F.|last2=Parisi|first2=Francesco|title=The Law and Economics of Cybersecurity|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-1-139-44696-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=toLwWiJt3m0C&pg=PA283|access-date=22 May 2017|language=en|date=2005-11-28}}</ref><!--https://books.google.com/books?id=E3PfuJmNuOcC-->

The topics of cyber peacekeeping<ref>{{cite arXiv|last1=Robinson|first1=Michael|last2=Janicke |first2=Helge|last3=Jones|first3=Kevin |title=An Introduction to Cyber Peacekeeping|eprint=1710.09616|class=cs.CY|year=2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Akatyev|first1=Nikolay|title=Digital Forensics and Cyber Crime|volume=157|pages=126–139|last2=James |first2=Joshua |chapter=Cyber Peacekeeping|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-25512-5_10|series=Lecture Notes of the Institute for Computer Sciences, Social Informatics and Telecommunications Engineering|year=2015|isbn=978-3-319-25511-8}}</ref> and cyber peacemaking<ref>{{cite book|last1=Ramsbotham|first1=Oliver|last2=Miall|first2=Hugh|last3=Woodhouse|first3=Tom|title=Contemporary Conflict Resolution|publisher=Polity|isbn=978-0-7456-4974-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-IbuQE02-KkC&pg=PA365|access-date=22 May 2017|language=en|date=2011-04-11}}</ref> have also been studied by researchers, as a way to restore and strengthen peace in the aftermath of both cyber and traditional warfare.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-07-19 |title=What are the challenges of cybersecurity in times of peace and war? |url=https://cyberpeaceinstitute.org/event/challenges-of-cybersecurity-in-times-of-war-and-peace/ |access-date=2022-11-08 |website=CyberPeace Institute |language=en-US}}</ref>

[https://foreignpolicy.com/2012/09/06/is-the-holy-grail-of-cyber-security-within-reach/ "Is the 'holy grail' of cyber security within reach?"]. ''Foreign Policy Magazine'', 6 September 2012.</ref>

== Doubts about existence ==
In October 2011 the ''[[Journal of Strategic Studies]]'', a leading journal in that field, published an article by [[Thomas Rid]], "Cyber War Will Not Take Place" which argued that all politically motivated cyber attacks are merely sophisticated versions of sabotage, espionage, or subversion – and that it is unlikely that cyber war will occur in the future.<ref name=":3">{{cite journal|last=Rid|first=Thomas|year=2012|title=Cyber War Will Not Take Place|journal=Journal of Strategic Studies|volume=35|issue=1 |pages=5–32|doi=10.1080/01402390.2011.608939|s2cid=153828543}}</ref>

== Legal perspective ==
NIST, a cybersecurity framework, was published in 2014 in the US.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2017-03-13 |title=Cybersecurity Framework |url=https://www.nist.gov/industry-impacts/cybersecurity-framework |journal=NIST |language=en |access-date=8 November 2022 |archive-date=8 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108034210/https://www.nist.gov/industry-impacts/cybersecurity-framework }}</ref>

The ''[[Tallinn Manual]]'', published in 2013, is an academic, non-binding study on how international law, in particular the [[jus ad bellum]] and [[international humanitarian law]], apply to cyber conflicts and [[cyber warfare]]. It was written at the invitation of the [[Tallinn]]-based [[NATO Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence]] by an international group of approximately twenty experts between 2009 and 2012.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tallinn manual 2.0 on the international law applicable to cyber operations |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/982063650 |access-date=2022-11-08 |website=WorldCat.org |language=en}}</ref>

The [[Shanghai Cooperation Organisation]] (members of which include China and Russia) defines cyberwar to include dissemination of information "harmful to the spiritual, moral and cultural spheres of other states". In September 2011, these countries proposed to the UN Secretary General a document called "International code of conduct for [[information security]]".<ref>Russian Embassy to the UK [http://www.rusemb.org.uk/policycontact/49]. Retrieved 25 May 2012.</ref>

In contrast, the United approach focuses on physical and economic damage and injury, putting political concerns under [[freedom of speech]]. This difference of opinion has led to reluctance in the West to pursue global cyber arms control agreements.<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=130052701 | title=Seeing The Internet As An 'Information Weapon' | publisher=NPR | first= Tom | last= Gjelten | date=23 September 2010 | access-date=23 September 2010 }}</ref> However, American General [[Keith B. Alexander]] did endorse talks with Russia over a proposal to limit military attacks in cyberspace.<ref>Gorman, Siobhan. (4 June 2010) [https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703340904575284964215965730?KEYWORDS=cybersecurity WSJ: U.S. Backs Talks on Cyber Warfare]. ''The Wall Street Journal''. Retrieved 8 November 2011.</ref> In June 2013, [[Barack Obama]] and [[Vladimir Putin]] agreed to install a secure ''Cyberwar-Hotline'' providing "a direct secure voice communications line between the US cybersecurity coordinator and the Russian deputy secretary of the security council, should there be a need to directly manage a crisis situation arising from an [[Information and communications technology|ICT]] security incident" (White House quote).<ref name="arshotline">Sean Gallagher, [https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2013/06/us-russia-to-install-cyber-hotline-to-prevent-accidental-cyberwar/ ''US, Russia to install "cyber-hotline" to prevent accidental cyberwar''], Arstechnica, 18 June 2013</ref>

A Ukrainian international law scholar, [[Alexander Merezhko]], has developed a project called the International Convention on Prohibition of Cyberwar in Internet. According to this project, cyberwar is defined as the use of Internet and related technological means by one state against the political, economic, technological and information sovereignty and independence of another state. Professor Merezhko's project suggests that the Internet ought to remain free from warfare tactics and be treated as an international landmark. He states that the Internet (cyberspace) is a "common heritage of mankind".<ref>[http://www.politik.org.ua/vid/publcontent.php3?y=7&p=57 Український центр політичного менеджменту – Зміст публікації – Конвенция о запрещении использования кибервойны] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111007185753/http://www.politik.org.ua/vid/publcontent.php3?y=7&p=57 |date=7 October 2011 }}. Politik.org.ua. Retrieved 8 November 2011.</ref>

On the February 2017 [[RSA Conference]] [[Microsoft]] president Brad Smith suggested global rules – a "Digital Geneva Convention" – for cyber attacks that "ban the nation-state hacking of all the civilian aspects of our economic and political infrastructures". He also stated that an independent organization could investigate and publicly disclose evidence that attributes nation-state attacks to specific countries. Furthermore, he said that the technology sector should collectively and neutrally work together to protect Internet users and pledge to [[corporate warfare|remain neutral in conflict]] and not aid governments in offensive activity and to adopt a coordinated disclosure process for software and hardware vulnerabilities.<ref>{{cite news|title='Digital Geneva Convention' needed to deter nation-state hacking: Microsoft president|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-microsoft-cyber-idUSKBN15T26V|work=Reuters|access-date=20 February 2017|date=14 February 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Kaspersky|first1=Eugene|title=A Digital Geneva Convention? A Great Idea.|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/eugenekaspersky/2017/02/15/a-digital-geneva-convention-a-great-idea/|website=Forbes|access-date=20 February 2017}}</ref> A fact-binding body has also been proposed to regulate cyber operations.<ref>"Regulating the Use and Conduct of Cyber Operations: Challenges and a Fact-Finding Body Proposal", https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3540615 (2019/2020)</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://digital-commons.usnwc.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2922&context=ils|title=An International Attribution Mechanism for Hostile Cyber Operations|author1=Yuval Shany |author2=Michael N. Schmitt|website=[[Naval War College]]|access-date=January 1, 2024}}</ref>

extract:
Cyberwarfare is the use of cyberattacks against an enemy state, causing comparable harm to traditional warfare. Some intended outcomes could be espionage, sabotage, propaganda, manipulation, or economic warfare.
Many countries, including the United States, United Kingdom, Russia, China, Israel, Iran, India, and North Korea, have active cyber capabilities for offensive and defensive operations. As states explore the use of cyber operations and combine capabilities, the likelihood of physical confrontation and violence playing out as a result of, or part of, a cyber operation is increased. However, meeting the scale and protracted nature of war is unlikely, thus ambiguity remains.
There has been significant debate among experts regarding the definition of cyberwarfare, and even if such a thing exists. One view is that the term is a misnomer, since no cyberattack to date could be described as a war. An alternative view is that it is a suitable label for cyberattacks that cause physical damage to people and objects in the real world.
The first instance of kinetic military action used in response to a cyberattack resulting in the loss of human life was observed on 5 May 2019, when the Israel Defense Forces targeted and destroyed a building associated with an ongoing cyberattack.
